Discrete Fourier transforms

Source: R/transform.R
fft_c2c.Rd

fft_c2c() computes the complex discrete Fourier transform of x or its inverse, fft_r2c() the transform of real input keeping only the non-redundant half of the last transformed axis, and fft_c2r() the inverse of fft_r2c(), returning real values. All three work over any subset of the dimensions of an array, in O(n log n) time for every length.

Usage

fft_c2c(
  x,
  inverse = FALSE,
  n = NULL,
  axes = NULL,
  norm = c("backward", "ortho", "forward", "none"),
  workers = NULL
)

fft_r2c(
  x,
  n = NULL,
  axes = NULL,
  norm = c("backward", "ortho", "forward", "none"),
  workers = NULL
)

fft_c2r(
  x,
  n = NULL,
  axes = NULL,
  norm = c("backward", "ortho", "forward", "none"),
  workers = NULL
)

Arguments

x

A double, integer, logical or complex vector or array. Integer and logical values are converted to double. fft_r2c() needs real input; fft_c2r() treats real input as complex.

inverse

TRUE for the inverse transform. 0 and 1 are accepted too, as in fftwtools.

n

Transform lengths, one per transformed axis (no recycling). Each axis of x is cropped or zero-padded to its length first. NULL keeps the lengths of x. For fft_c2r(), n gives the lengths of the real output; the last transformed axis of x must then hold n %/% 2 + 1 values and is cropped or padded to that. Its default is 2 * (m - 1) for an input extent m, which is always even: give n to recover an odd length.

axes

The dimensions to transform, 1-based, without repeats. NULL means all of them, in order. For the real transforms the last listed axis is the one that is halved. Use axes = 1 for a column-wise transform of a matrix, as stats::mvfft() does.

norm

Where the scaling goes. "backward" (the default) leaves the forward transform unscaled and divides the inverse by N, the product of the transformed lengths; "forward" does the opposite; "ortho" divides both by sqrt(N); "none" scales neither direction, as FFTW, fftwtools and stats::fft() do.

workers

Threads to use. NULL uses the session default (1). Negative values count back from the number of available cores: -1 means all of them. Requests are capped at the available cores, and at 2 when _R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_ is set. Threads split the independent 1-D transforms of a multi-dimensional array, so they help only arrays with at least 32 768 elements and more than one line. Results agree to rounding whatever the number of threads; they are bit-identical on builds without fused multiply-add (CRAN's x86-64 builds).

Value

For fft_c2c() and fft_r2c() a complex vector or array, for fft_c2r() a double one. Arrays keep their dim, with the transformed extents, and the dimnames of axes that were not transformed; names are dropped.

Details

The conventions are those of scipy.fft (fft, fftn, rfftn, irfftn): n crops or zero-pads each transformed axis before the transform, and norm chooses where the scaling goes. They differ from SciPy in two ways: axes are 1-based, and axes = NULL means every dimension rather than the last one.

Speed: R stores arrays column by column, so the first axis is the contiguous one, whereas in NumPy it is the last. The real transforms halve the last listed axis, as SciPy does; listing the first axis last, for example fft_r2c(m, axes = 2:1) for a matrix, halves the contiguous axis and is often much faster (about 1.8 times for a 2048 x 2048 matrix).

Coming from fftwtools: fft_c2c(x) is fftw(x) and fftw_r2c(x), fft_r2c(x) is fftw_r2c(x, HermConj = 0), and an fftwtools inverse is the zufft inverse with norm = "none", because fftwtools, like stats::fft(), never scales.

See also

stats::fft() for R's own complex transform.

Other transforms: fft_dct()

Examples

x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2)
fft_c2c(x)
#> [1]  1.500000e+01+0i -4.000000e+00+0i -2.220446e-16+0i -1.000000e+00+0i
#> [5] -2.220446e-16+0i -4.000000e+00+0i
fft_r2c(x)
#> [1]  1.500000e+01+0i -4.000000e+00+0i -2.220446e-16+0i -1.000000e+00+0i
fft_c2r(fft_r2c(x), n = length(x))
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 3 2

# an inverse that matches fftwtools and stats::fft(inverse = TRUE)
fft_c2c(fft_c2c(x), inverse = TRUE, norm = "none") / length(x)
#> [1] 1+0i 2+0i 3+0i 4+0i 3+0i 2+0i

# columns of a matrix, and both axes
m <- matrix(rnorm(12), 4, 3)
fft_c2c(m, axes = 1)
#>                      [,1]                 [,2]                  [,3]
#> [1,] -3.587561+0.0000000i -0.2991786+0.000000i -0.4516224+0.0000000i
#> [2,]  1.037220-0.2608883i  2.4433704-1.395737i  0.3094998+0.9116875i
#> [3,] -4.087053+0.0000000i -2.1013512+0.000000i -1.1441756+0.0000000i
#> [4,]  1.037220+0.2608883i  2.4433704+1.395737i  0.3094998-0.9116875i
fft_r2c(m)
#>                      [,1]                 [,2]
#> [1,] -4.338362+0.0000000i -3.212161-0.1320202i
#> [2,]  3.790090-0.7449378i -2.337503-1.8668498i
#> [3,] -7.332580+0.0000000i -2.464289+0.8289384i
#> [4,]  3.790090+0.7449378i  1.659073-1.8291225i
